title: STAT+: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy gets its first FDA-approved drug, from BridgeBio
summary: A type of muscular dystrophy that was long ignored has its first drug — and it could earn BridgeBio a billion dollars a year.
text:
The Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved the first drug to treat limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, a broad collection of progressive muscle conditions that has long received scant attention from physicians and drug developers.
The drug, developed by BridgeBio under the name ribitol and marketed as Welgemda, is specifically approved for patients with LGMD 2i/R9, a subtype the company estimates affects 2,000 to 3,000 patients in the U.S. and another 4,000 to 5,000 in Europe.
BridgeBio said Monday it will charge insurers $75,446.58 for a 28-day supply of medicine — meaning the price will be just a hair under $1 million per year.

title: ‘Smart’ Implants Are Driving Up Health Costs — Even When Patients Don’t Ask for Them
summary: Two patients are suing after allegedly waking from knee replacement surgery and learning they’d received “smart” joints, capable of transmitting data. Researchers say their usefulness is unproven, yet Medicare and private insurers pay doctors to monitor such devices.
text:
‘Smart’ Implants Are Driving Up Health Costs — Even When Patients Don’t Ask for Them
Steve Russak, 70, of Santa Rosa Valley, California, woke up from knee replacement surgery last year to a text message. It was from the company that made his new knee. Over the next few days, the company, Zimmer Biomet, texted four times. Russak didn’t understand the inquiries asking him to use an app, he said.
Finally, a company representative called and offered help setting up some accessories, Russak told KFF Health News. “I said, ‘What? I don’t know what you’re talking about.’”
It turned out Russak did not receive just any old replacement of bone and cartilage. He’d had a “smart knee” put in — an artificial joint called the Persona IQ with a lithium-ion battery, sensors, and transmitter that, should he authorize it, would send data about his gait and range of motion to his clinicians and Zimmer.
Russak is suing the doctor, Zimmer, and Canary Medical, a health technology company that helped develop the device. In his lawsuit, Russak claims the knee was an “unauthorized implantation” and that, according to Zimmer’s “patient-facing materials,” he should have been given the option to opt out of data collection or decline the knee altogether, but wasn’t.
Russak said he doesn’t want to set up the device to collect and transmit data for several reasons, including his privacy. Now that it’s in his body, though, he said it poses potential disruptions. For example, Russak said he recently couldn’t get an MRI because of compatibility issues.
Neither the doctor nor the doctor’s lawyer responded to multiple requests for comment.
The case is ongoing, with the next hearing scheduled for December. Russak said he has dropped the fraud and breach of fiduciary duty allegations originally filed against the doctor but is continuing to sue on other grounds, including lack of informed consent. The doctor has yet to respond to the complaint in court.
Both Zimmer and Canary filed initial responses denying “each and every allegation” in Russak’s complaint. They have offered a variety of defenses, including that any damages are the fault of another party or, as Zimmer’s response said, caused by actions or reactions “not reasonably foreseeable.”
Canary Medical did not respond to requests for comment. Zimmer spokesperson Troy Kirkpatrick declined to comment on lawsuits against the company but said that “nearly 90%” of surveyed patients who received Zimmer’s joint replacements report they would choose an orthopedic device with remote monitoring capabilities again in the future.
“The transmission of post-operative recovery data requires patient authorization at the time the patient sets up an account and is designed to support patient-surgeon relationships and postoperative care,” Kirkpatrick said in an emailed statement. He added that Zimmer takes privacy and compliance with regulations “very seriously.”

title: Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
summary: The jump in Nvidia shares has also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq up 6.5%.
text:
Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
- Published
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.
His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.
Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.
Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday, with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.
Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.
Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.
While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.
A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.
On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.
Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.
Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".
"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.
"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.
"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.

title: ‘Medicare for All’ Is Back on Drawing Board. Does It Stand a Better Chance This Time?
summary: Some incoming lawmakers told voters they’d fight for universal, government-funded health coverage. Julie Rovner, KFF Health News’ chief Washington correspondent, writes about what the coming health debate has in common with past fights — and something that’s different this time around.
text:
History doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That’s certainly true of the coming fight over “Medicare for All.”
The midterm elections saw victories by several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail.
But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there have cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act — which, despite incendiary politics, made incremental reforms — barely squeaked into law after similar disputes in 2009.
And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem.
‘It’s Cosplay’
So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish?
For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase “Medicare for All” actually means. “It’s cosplay,” said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. “When you say ‘Medicare for All,’ people think ‘Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.’”
Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF’s public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters.
“I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs,” she said of survey respondents’ support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. “I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program.”
			
The predicted blue wave in the 2026 midterms not only appeared — it overperformed, with Democrats sweeping into majorities in the House and Senate. That sets up a new focus on health policy, with Democrats seeking to undo cuts imposed by President Donald Trump and the GOP-led Congress and advance their own agenda to increase coverage and lower costs. title: Trump claims credit as Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
summary: President Trump endorsed the announcement, calling it essential for the success of the company and the economy. He added that the government does not see Jensen's return as a national security risk.
text:
Trump claims credit as Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR.
Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO of the world's largest chipmaker on Monday, sending the company's stock soaring as President Trump claimed credit for brokering his close ally's return.
It was a stunning reversal of fortune for Huang. He resigned less than two weeks ago, following news reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy.
In a statement put out just before the market opened, Nvidia said its board voted unanimously in favor of bringing back Huang after a series of conversations and meetings, as well as input from people at "senior levels" of the U.S. government. "Based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk," the board said.
Nvidia's stock price shot up more than 30% on Monday, helping buoy stock indexes after last week's losses, which were driven by the tech sector.
Trump endorsed the board's move, calling it the "correct and proper decision" in a social media post. He said Huang's leadership was needed "in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."
The president had repeatedly urged Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang as CEO in public comments and on social media. In a lengthy interview with CNBC Monday morning, Trump claimed his influence helped Huang get his job back.
"I don't want to say, but basically I was represented at the board," the president said, in response to a question about a report in Semafor that he had called directly into the NVIDIA board meeting.
"I spoke to them. Let me just put it that way. And I convinced them," Trump told CNBC. "And I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago."
He later added: "When the stock starts dropping forty, fifty percent, it was a lot easier for me to do it yesterday than it would have been."
Huang stepped down amid a growing scandal
Nvidia, which Huang co-founded and has run for the past 33 years, dominates the market for the chips used to train and run artificial intelligence. Trump and Huang have grown close during the president's second term in office, with Huang becoming one of the most influential business leaders with the president's ear on AI policy. He has successfully lobbied the U.S. government to allow chipmakers to sell some chips to China, although Nvidia's most advanced chips are subject to export controls.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12 after news reports that he had affairs with multiple women, including an Nvidia executive who reported to him. But the most explosive allegation was that he'd engaged in a relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia chips, whom U.S. officials believed had ties to Chinese intelligence.

title: STAT+: Pharmalittle: We’re reading about Capricor’s Duchenne drug, Lilly’s 15th acquisition of 2026, and more
summary: The FDA again rejected a hotly debated experimental Duchenne muscular dystrophy drug from Capricor Therapeutics
text:
Good morning, Jason Mast here filling in from Pharmalot’s Midtown Bureau. Wishing you a happy Turkey week. I hope that it is joyful, or at least tolerable. In the meantime, the news marches on. …
The FDA again rejected a hotly debated experimental Duchenne muscular dystrophy drug from Capricor Therapeutics, STAT tells us. The rejection letter came months after an advisory committee in which reviewers excoriated the company’s data, saying a Phase 3 trial had — contrary to Capricor’s claims — clearly failed. Some advocates and doctors pushed for the drug’s approval, noting it was for patients with a terminal disease and few other options.
Eli Lilly bought a U.K.-based Huntington’s disease startup for up to $725 million, Endpoints reports. The startup, called LoQus23 Therapeutics, is developing a pill aimed at an increasingly popular target in neurons called MSH3. LoQus23 planned to start a human trial in the coming months. This is Lilly’s 15th acquisition of the year, as its leaders look to pour obesity-drug riches into a new wave of powerful medicines.
Kymera said its closely watched Dupixent rival safely and effectively treated eczema in a Phase 2 study, STAT relays. The pill, called KT-621, targets an inflammatory protein called STAT6. It is among the first of a new kind of therapy called protein degraders that chemists and executives hope will let them target previously undruggable proteins. KT-621 has generated particular excitement among investors because of its potential to serve as an oral alternative to Dupixent, Sanofi and Regeneron’s mega-blockbuster immune drug.

title: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
summary: Older drivers are using Tesla's automated driving technology to stay on the road longer. But safety experts warn the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.
text:
Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals.
Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.
"I just get in and go," Spalding says.
For all practical purposes, the car appears to be driving itself, navigating confidently on twisting roads through postcard valleys full of juniper and ponderosa pine.
"Now this is probably one of the narrowest roads," Spalding says, as the car pulls onto a dirt track that can barely fit two cars side by side, with a steep drop off to one side.
The Tesla handles the tight turns gracefully, even stopping to let an SUV squeeze by in the other lane.
Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's a subscription service that drivers pay for, usually $99 dollars per month.
That was, until she saw what it could do.
"When I was driving," Spalding said, "I saw that the kind of things that it did were safer than what I would do."
There are more older drivers on the road than ever, and families often struggle with the question of when it's time to stop driving. Now, seniors are using emerging technology to stay behind the wheel longer, specifically automated systems made by Tesla. But safety experts worry the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.
"It's not a technology that I would drive with. It's not a technology that I would suggest that my loved ones use. I think it has a few safety gaps that just make me uncomfortable," said Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT, who studies how drivers interact with technology.
It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing. Overall, Tesla says FSD has more than 1.7 million active subscriptions, an increase of 67% from a year ago. If the car-maker knows how many of those subscribers are seniors, it isn't saying.
Riding along with Joan Spalding, it's easy to understand the appeal for older drivers. The car gives her mobility and freedom that she wouldn't have otherwise.
Before she got her Tesla, Spalding had gotten into a number of minor fender benders. Then, two years ago, she was in a serious crash while she was trying to make a left turn.
"I made a wrong decision. I wasn't focusing on what I should be doing … I was lucky," she said. "But I realized then that my abilities were not where I wanted them to be."
Her son Mike Spalding had known for a while that his mother's driving was getting worse. He was already driving a Tesla, and it was his idea to get one for her.

title: Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
summary: Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms says he will recommend major reforms to the personal independence payment.
text:
Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
- Published
A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.
Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits in England and Wales for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".
Writing in the Times, external, he said his review, to be published on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".
It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.
Sir Stephen, who produced his report alongside disability groups, carers, clinicians and MPs, said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.
He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".
"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases.
"Where claimants do not have additional costs or care needs, we should be signposting them to services and support."
He added: "Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary.
"Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."
The Timms review was commissioned after a U-turn from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government on a plan for major benefit reform, which attempted to reduce the welfare bill by £5bn a year.
More than 130 MPs, including 120 from Labour, signed an amendment to reject plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments in 2025.
The rebels said they opposed the plans because of the number of people expected to be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation at the time.
- Number of people claiming key disability benefit hits record high 
  - Published15 September
Sir Stephen's long-awaited review comes only a week after a former Labour Health Secretary Alan Milburn handed down his proposed reforms to tackle youth unemployment.
The government welcomed the Milburn review, which included a recommendation to move those aged 18 to 24 off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he thought the "same philosophy" could be applied "right through the age range".
At this stage it is unclear how both of the reviews will complement one another.

title: At first preventive services panel meeting in more than a year, votes are cast in private
summary: In its first meeting since 2025, an influential panel of doctors evaluating preventive medical care grappled with the ways RFK Jr. has upended science and medicine:
text:
Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
I’m taking a (very basic, 101) biochemistry course, and I spent much of the weekend trying to memorize the steps of glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. Metabolism is a beast, and I welcome your mnemonics!
In exchange, I offer a glimpse inside the two-day meeting of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, which hasn’t met in more than a year. Members (many of them new and appointed by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.) grappled with how to apply the Trump administration’s DEI rules to recommendations on cervical cancer screening and perinatal depression, among other things. Read on.
At first preventive services panel meeting in more than a year, votes are cast in private
In its first meeting since March 2025, an influential panel of doctors that evaluates preventive medical care grappled with the ways Kennedy has upended science and medicine.
Last week, the 16-member panel voted on recommendations on screening for cervical cancer, perinatal depression, and unhealthy alcohol use by teens and adults. The recommendations have been awaiting completion for more than a year while Kennedy repeatedly canceled meetings and largely remade the panel’s membership.
The discussion was livestreamed to the public for the first time, though the votes were held in private. Throughout the session, longtime and new members debated a Trump administration policy requiring the removal of language on “diversity, equity, and inclusion,” after Roger Klein, director of the USPSTF’s parent organization, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, cut all sub-population data from recommendation language.
“I worry that having edits from political leadership on the topline may lead to the perception that the task force recommendations are no longer scientifically independent,” Alicia Fernandez, a member of the panel since 2025, said as members discussed cervical cancer screenings.
At another point, some members expressed concern about bias in the presentations from subject matter experts. Members also asked how they might accurately and transparently explain when and how artificial intelligence is used in their data and recommendations.
“Should our documentation say ‘supported by AI?’” new member Ronald Karlsberg asked. — Chelsea Cirruzzo

Patients.
Experts say the impact of the ADA’s crisis won’t be felt immediately. But a dysfunctional professional organization could stymie advances in diabetes care for years to come. title: Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
summary: Huang's role at the centre of his company's journey to lynchpin of AI proved crucial.
text:
Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
- Published
There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.
The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.
Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.
The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning.
The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.
All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history.
This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.
The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.
And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board.
This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September, where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.
Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument.
There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.
Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.
This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.
The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.
Nvidia's stock market valuation has been used as a critical form of financing for other companies to construct data centres.
A complex web of loans, guarantees, and shareholdings helped spread and sustain the AI boom. Jensen Huang's exit had raised doubts about the fragility of this system, and the interim management had suggested a more "disciplined and selective" approach.
The concerns about so-called "circular financing" still raise concerns from some analysts. The public backlash against datacentres and AI evident at the US midterm elections also point to a changed environment.

title: STAT+: Invivyd reports positive results in Sisyphean Covid antibody quest
summary: The biotech Invivyd reported that its monoclonal antibody strongly protected people from Covid. Is there a market for it?
text:
An experimental monoclonal antibody showed 70% to 90% protection against symptomatic Covid-19, Invivyd, a small biotech firm, said Monday.
The result, from a 2,359-volunteer clinical trial called DECLARATION, included three arms: a single 250-mg dose of the antibody, VYD2311; monthly doses of VYD2311; or a saline placebo. Results were released by press release. Invivyd said that it plans to file for accelerated approval for VYD2311 for preventing symptomatic Covid.
During the pandemic, monoclonal antibodies were employed both as treatments and preventatives for Covid. The technology, however, fell into disuse as the market shrank and people gained protection against the infection. Still, Covid causes tens of thousands of deaths in the U.S., and Invivyd executives argued that there is a need for a monoclonal antibody. Moreover, they say, for some patients the monoclonal could be more effective than existing Covid vaccines. Covid vaccines reduced symptomatic infection by about 30%.
“Clinically, I really do believe that most Americans who are interested in using a pharmacological agent to protect themselves from Covid would probably move over to a monoclonal if given the option,” said Michael Mina, the former Harvard University infectious disease expert who is Invivyd’s chief medical officer. “And I think we’re going to aim to have volumes that can accommodate that over the coming couple of years.”

title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
summary: The Nvidia chief executive has been at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom.
text:
How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
- Published
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.
No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.
The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.
Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.
Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.
Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry.
That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potential rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned.
Spider's web of financing
The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".
Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.
The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

title: STAT+: Kymera Therapeutics reports mid-stage eczema trial success for would-be Dupixent rival
summary: Kymera Therapeutics announced on Monday that its experimental therapy effectively and safely treated eczema patients’ itchy, inflamed skin.
text:
In a closely watched trial seen as one of this year’s most impactful immunology drug readouts, Kymera Therapeutics announced on Monday that its experimental therapy effectively and safely treated eczema patients’ itchy, inflamed skin.
In the Phase 2 trial, moderate-to-severe eczema patients randomly assigned to receive the biotech’s pill, KT-621, showed a statistically significant reduction in disease severity compared with those given a placebo. This was true across all three doses tested after 16 weeks of treatment, with a peak placebo-adjusted improvement of 45% among those given a moderate dose. Patients on this dose were also more likely to see an improvement of 75% or more in disease severity, with 62% of treated participants clearing that bar compared with 22% of the placebo group.
The BROADEN2 trial succeeded across all primary and secondary endpoints, including itch reduction and the fraction of patients who achieved clear or almost-clear skin. KT-621 was also generally safe and well tolerated. The only side effect that was more common among patients on the drug was conjunctivitis (i.e. pink eye), which appeared in 20%, 13%, and 11% of patients on a low, middle, and high dose, respectively. All of these cases were mild to moderate, and none caused participants to stop treatment.

title: The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
summary: Days after resigning while mired in scandal of extra-marital affairs, Nvidia's Jensen Huang is making a remarkable return.
text:
The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
- Published
It's being called a comeback for the ages.
For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.
Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.
Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.
So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.
But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.
The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.
His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.
Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.
The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.
So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

title: STAT+: New biotech aims to develop next generation CAR-T for multiple myeloma
summary: Relapse in multiple myeloma is common. A new type of CAR-T aims to avoid that by adding a target to evade the tumor.
text:
Multiple myeloma patients have been able to utilize a surge of powerful new immunotherapies in recent years, including CAR-T therapy and bispecific antibodies like Carvykti and Tecvayli from Johnson & Johnson. But myeloma, a blood cancer, can often develop resistance against these treatments, leading to relapse.
A new biotech called Caronilex is developing a next generation CAR-T therapy that may help circumvent that resistance, and the therapy’s promising safety profile could make it a potential candidate for use against autoimmune diseases as well.
Researchers showed the therapy, called TriPRIL, was able to reduce or eliminate signs of cancer in 12 of 15 patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, many of whom had prior CAR-T therapy, in a small, early phase trial published last week in The Lancet.

title: Opinion: If the AI bubble bursts, it could create a serious problem for health care
summary: “A health AI company's market value and the medical value of its technology are two different things,” writes David Adler.
text:
The Oct. 30 sell-off on Wall Street ignited doubts about whether the huge investment in artificial intelligence will earn the returns investors expect. Those concerns have persisted, with even Anthropic’s initial public offering on Nov. 19 failing to halt the broader tech sell-off.
If the AI bubble bursts (assuming it is a bubble) and takes some medical AI companies down with it, health care will face a serious problem. A health AI company’s market value and the medical value of its technology are two different things. If funding runs out because investors decide to walk away, hospitals could lose the chance to complete evaluations of potentially useful medical tools. Giving up on medical AI would be a financial decision — but it may look like a clinical one. The financial markets will decide which medical AI technologies survive before hospitals have had the opportunity to establish whether these technologies benefit patients.
If investment in medical AI technologies experiences a sharp fall, companies will lose funding, forcing them to reduce their activities or stop supporting their technologies completely. The impact of such an event could be felt across the entire health care system: Companies are developing AI tools ranging from interpreting scans to identifying patients at risk of developing medical complications due to treatments. Clearly, some of these tools will eventually prove useful in clinical settings, while others will not. The point is that neither an impressive AI tool nor a falling stock price tells us which AI tool deserves a place within the health care system.
To illustrate this point, let’s take cancer clinical trials as an example. In one study, researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Emory University examined electronic medical records using AI systems to identify patients who may meet the eligibility criteria for inclusion in clinical trials. Determining eligibility involves a demanding manual screening process examining things like tumor characteristics, previous treatments, and lab results.
Interestingly, the findings revealed that using the AI system improved accuracy of assessing enrollment eligibility for the cancer clinical trials, but it didn’t reduce screening time significantly. It’s not clear whether such improvements would lead to an increase in patient enrollment. In another study, researchers in Australia from the Victorian Cancer Registry at Cancer Council Victoria and Monash Health utilized an AI system to analyze pathology reports with the goal of identifying patients eligible for enrollment in cancer clinical trials. The AI system was able to successfully identify more eligible patients when compared to standard screening procedures, but ultimately utilizing the AI system didn’t result in increased patient enrollment into the clinical trials. The study didn’t establish why, which brings to focus that screening improvements doesn’t necessarily lead to higher clinical trial participation.
